tiles.alt: CHAPTER FOUR / The Efficient Market Hypothesis

The great marble banking hall of Gringotts, lit by tall windows and candle chandeliers. Goblin clerks scribble at a long high counter. / Inside, it was marble and gold and hush, and the clerks were not human.
One of them looked down at Harry over his spectacles as if pricing him.

A mine cart hurtles through dark caverns. Harry has both arms up, thrilled. McGonagall grips her hat. Somewhere in the dark, something large with an orange eye watches. / Harry: IS THIS A ROLLER COASTER?! / clatter clatter clatter
The Potter vault: mountains of gold coins glittering in torchlight, and Harry, very small, staring. / Heaps of gold Galleons. Stacks of silver Sickles. Piles of bronze Knuts.

From the doorway, Professor McGonagall watched him—leaning casually against the wall, but with her eyes intent. / Being plopped in front of a giant heap of gold coins was a test of character so pure it was archetypal.
Harry: Are these coins the pure metal?
Griphook: Are you questioning the integrity of Gringotts, Mr Potter-Evans-Verres?

Harry: No! Not at all. Sorry if that came out wrong, sir. I just have no idea how your financial system works. / Harry: Can anyone coin Galleons? Or are they issued by a monopoly that thereby collects seigniorage?
McGonagall: What? / Griphook: Only a fool would trust any but goblin coin!

Harry: Suppose I came in here with a ton of silver. Could I get a ton of Sickles made from it? / Griphook: For a fee, Mr Potter-Evans-Verres. For a certain fee. Where would you find a ton of silver, I wonder?
Harry: I was speaking hypothetically. Give me a wild guess—what fraction would you charge? / Griphook: A twentieth part of the metal would well pay for the coining.

Harry's pencil diagram: silver → Sickles → Galleons → gold sold in Muggle London → more silver than you started with. Repeat forever. / So not only is the wizarding economy almost completely decoupled from the Muggle economy—no-one here has ever heard of arbitrage.
One competent hedge fund manager could probably own the whole wizarding world within a week. Harry filed the notion away, in case he ever ran out of money, or had a week free.
McGonagall: I think that will be more than enough to pay for your school supplies, Mr Potter. / Harry: Hm? Hold on, I'm doing a Fermi calculation.
McGonagall: A what?
Harry's Fermi estimate in pencil: twenty Galleons weigh about a tenth of a kilo, so a Galleon is about fifty pounds; five pyramid-shaped mounds come to about two million pounds.
Harry: Not bad. / Harry: That's the last time I ever mow a lawn for one lousy pound.

Harry: Pardon me for asking, Professor, but is this a usual amount of money for a young couple to have? / McGonagall: Your father was the last heir of an old family. And… some of it may be from bounties placed on You-Know-Who. / McGonagall: Payable to whoever might defeat him.

Harry: Interesting… So some of this really is, in a sense, mine. Earned by me. Sort of. Possibly. / Harry: That makes me feel less guilty about spending a very tiny fraction of it! / Harry: DON'T PANIC, PROFESSOR McGONAGALL!
McGonagall: Mr Potter! You are a minor! You will only be allowed to make reasonable withdrawals—

Harry: I am all about reasonable! I am totally on board with fiscal prudence and impulse control! / Harry: But I did see some things on the way here which would constitute sensible, grown-up purchases…
McGonagall: Like what?
Harry: Trunks whose insides hold more than their outsides? / Harry: When I'm an adult I'll want one anyway. And I can afford one. It's the same money either way, right?
McGonagall: And just what would you keep in a trunk like that, Mr Potter—
Harry: Books. / McGonagall: Of course.
Harry: And I'll make the deal sweeter! Hogwarts can keep some of the books I bring, for the library. It's okay to bribe people with books, right? That's a—
McGonagall: Family tradition. / Harry: Yes, exactly!

McGonagall: I cannot deny the sense of your words, though I much wish I could. I will allow you an additional hundred Galleons. / McGonagall: I know that I shall regret this, and I am doing it anyway.

Harry: That's the spirit! And does a "mokeskin pouch" do what I think it does? / Harry: It would be like Batman's utility belt of holding! I could have the top three books I'm reading on me at all times! It's for the sake of children's reading, the best of all possible causes!
McGonagall: …I suppose you may add another ten Galleons. / Griphook was favouring Harry with a gaze of frank respect.
Harry: And a little spending money, like you mentioned earlier. I think I remember seeing one or two other things—
McGonagall: Don't push it, Mr Potter.

Harry: But oh, Professor McGonagall, why rain on my parade? Surely this is a happy day, when I discover all things wizarding for the first time! / Harry: Why not smile and remember your own innocent childhood, watching the delight upon my young face as I buy a few toys using an insignificant fraction of the wealth I earned by defeating the most terrible wizard Britain has ever known—not that I'm accusing you of being ungrateful or anything—
McGonagall's face, backlit in red, is fearsome and terrible. / McGonagall: You.
Harry squeaked, stepped back, and sprawled backwards into a heap of money. Griphook put a palm over his face.
McGonagall: I would be doing a great service to wizarding Britain, Mr Potter, if I locked you in this vault and left you here.
And they left without any more trouble.
Close on Harry's trouser pocket, bulging with gold coins he scooped up when he fell. / clink / Not quite without any more trouble.

A tiny shop crammed with hanging pouches. A nervous young witch in faded yellow robes shows Harry a furry pouch. / The Moke Shop was a quaint little shop behind a vegetable stall behind a glove shop, down an alleyway off a side street of Diagon Alley. / Keeper: The Moke Super Pouch QX31! Widening Lip and an Undetectable Extension Charm.
Harry: Can I try this for a bit? To make sure it works, um, reliably? / He widened his eyes in an expression of boyish, playful innocence.
"bag of gold" / "bag of gold" / "bag of gold" / After ten repetitions, Professor McGonagall wandered off to examine the other items in the shop, and the shopkeeper turned to watch her.
Harry: The golden coins were his. But they were still stolen. Self-stolen? Auto-thieved? / Harry: About thirty Galleons, he guessed.
As they leave, the shop door grows a wooden hand and waves. / The door formed a hand and waved goodbye to them, which made Harry feel a bit queasy.

An old man with a cane, one huge tear on his cheek. / Old man: Are you really Harry Potter? You wouldn't lie about that, would you? / Old man: Only I'd heard rumours that you didn't really survive, and that's why no-one ever heard from you again.
Professor McGonagall yanked Harry into the nearest alleyway. / Harry: I only know what other people have told me. It's not like I remember being born.
Harry: If there's already sufficient cause to postulate a conspiracy, there's no reason they wouldn't just find another orphan and raise him to believe he was Harry Potter—

McGonagall: You look just about exactly like your father, the year he first came to Hogwarts. / McGonagall: And I can attest on the basis of personality alone that you are related to the Scourge of Gryffindor.
Harry: She could be in on it too.
Old man: No. She's right. You have your mother's eyes.
Harry: Hmm. I suppose you could be in on it too— / McGonagall: Enough, Mr Potter.
Old man: I'm just glad that you're alive. Thank you, Harry Potter. Thank you for what you did. / Old man: I'll leave you alone now.
The old man taps slowly away out of the alley. / tap… tap… tap…
McGonagall: That was not well done. I know you're not used to this, Mr Potter, but people do care about you. Please be kind to them. / Harry: They shouldn't. Care about me, I mean.
McGonagall: You saved them from You-Know-Who. How should they not care?
Harry: I suppose there's no chance that if I said "fundamental attribution error" you'd have any idea what that meant.
McGonagall: No. But please explain, Mr Potter, if you would be so kind.
"When we look at other people, we see personality traits. When we look at ourselves, we see circumstances."
Pencil diagram: on the left a stick figure kicking a desk, labelled "what an angry person!"; on the right, the same man being shoved into a wall on his way to work.

Harry: People think I saved them from You-Know-Who because I have some kind of permanent, enduring destroy-the-Dark-Lord trait. / Harry: I was fifteen months old! They don't care about me. They want to shake hands with a bad explanation.
Harry: Do you know what really happened?
McGonagall: I have formed an idea… After meeting you, that is. / Harry: Yes?
McGonagall: You triumphed over the Dark Lord by being more awful than he was, and survived the Killing Curse by being more terrible than Death.
Harry: Ha. Ha. Ha.
McGonagall: Let's get you to Madam Malkin's next. I fear your Muggle clothing may be attracting attention.

Madam Malkin's robe shop, plain and respectable. / Madam Malkin's Robes for All Occasions. A genuinely boring shop front: red brick, plain black robes in the window, and the door propped wide open as if to advertise that there was nothing to hide.
